subject: Map genetic sub-group of cohort with incomplete testing.

messages.author: f9c6a2087c744460
messages.subject: Map genetic sub-group of cohort with incomplete testing.
parts:
Dear INLA experts,

The background: We have a set of about 2,250 cases from a population disease register, and combining with census data have produced maps via the BYM model. For about 50% of cases we have data regarding testing a specific gene that causes about 10% of the cases. So out of 2,250 cases, about 1000 were genetically tested and roughly 100 tested +ve with 900 -ve. The people who got tested are probably spatially biased to be living closer to research centres. I have been asked to produce a map of spatial incidence of where this gene occurs (if possible). However I don't know how to do this given not every case was tested.

Is there any clever way of using inla to produce such a map? Although I have been working with the BYM model I'm wondering could I treat data as point patterns for this purpose. For example I see in the spde book section 4.3 geostatistics under preferential sampling. Could the preferential sampling approach be adapted to point pattern data instead of geostatistics?

I appreciate any thoughts folks might have. 
Thanks,
James

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Map genetic sub-group of cohort with incomplete testing.
parts:
Hi,

Your issue looks very similar to the types of models used in ecology for transect sampling, where the probability of observing an animal depends on its distance to the observer.  Such models tend to lead to nonlinear predictor models that can’t be run directly in inla, but can be defined and estimated in the inlabru package (which was developed partly for this precise reason).  In the workshop tutorial material on inlabru.org we look at Poisson point process models, with observation models modulated by detection probability models.
I’m not sure your problem would be best described using Poisson process formalism, but the same idea can be applied for measurements (0/1 detection indicators) observed at fixed locations.  The other preferential sampling modelling techniques might also be combined with this; if you can formulate a model for the data-generation process, it would be easier to figure out what implementation approach would be suitable.

Finn

Finn

> Another issue is of course also that you only have data from cases, so wouldn’t necessarily contain information about the spatial distribution of the gene in the population as a whole; it would be conditionally on having the disease.

Yes this has occurred to me also. I was wondering if I could use treat the posterior estimates from my BYM model as a continuous field (so spatial field of relative risk of getting the disease regardless of genetics), and then jointly model that with the genetic data somehow? Alas, I'm unsure if this would be mathematically sound.
What do you think ?
James
